title: Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames
author: Nick Ames at Old Trafford
text:
There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe

Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.

Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.

Until United are equipped to repeat their second 45 minutes on a weekly basis, which requires systemic change in departments far outside the technical area, even if Carrick’s head will surely be first on the block, nobody is likely to deliver them from ongoing psychodrama. History may tell that his heavily maligned players were fruitlessly raging against the dying of the light in blowing Roma out of the water. But their achievement here was worth savouring for its discreet brilliance and, perhaps, the wholesome powers that ultimately wrought it.

Kobbie Mainoo had been introduced as “Manchester born and bred”, to obligatory cheers, when the teams were read out. Any emotional heartstring is worth plucking on at the moment but there was something grounding about seeing the midfielder, largely injured over the past month and an onlooker while his colleagues’ fortunes spiralled, return to the starting XI. Mainoo was far from alone in enduring a tentative, twitchy, flustered first half but was caught flat-footed when Marten de Roon mugged him near halfway, setting in train the move that exposed an execrably organised backline for Matías Soulé’s opener.

At 2-0, another crossfield ball from the left having triggered United’s defence into recidivism, Mainoo attempted to raise spirits by surging through the middle on his own and spraying the ball right under pressure. There was no more nourishing gruel on offer than this; the only nagging glimmer of possibility was that Roma, for all their broad control, did not look like the kind of side that would withstand any gale that came their way.

When Carlos Baleba, eye-catching in phases but loose in possession, pulled up with Bryan Mbeumo ready for a tap-in, the notes of misery deepened. But the subsequent introduction of Youri Tielemans, in his element against opponents whose intensity was evidently sagging, created angles and spaces that had previously seemed figments of the mind. United were fortunate when Bruno Fernandes converted his soft, twice-taken penalty; they were gifted parity when Leonardo Balerdi’s air-kick afforded Matheus Cunha a chance he could barely miss. The die, though, had long been cast through their waves of slick, insistent pressure.

So it fell for Mainoo and another academy product, Shea Lacey, to tee up the coup de grace. Lacey hails from Liverpool but there is no need to whisper that: his credentials since childhood have firmly passed muster. While Lisandro Martínez was lightly booed on to the pitch in the 75th minute, Lacey arrived with him to raptures. How poetic it was that Mainoo, speeding up an attack before quickly shifting the ball right, and the mesmerising Lacey, should complete the revival.

Lacey’s jink inside and left-footed pass whipped into Cunha were genuinely breathtaking. So was the finish and so, too, the reaction. Few do it quite like an Old Trafford crowd on a European night. This is still a citadel like no other, even if its strains nowadays alternate between dubbing Mainoo unplayable and impolitely requesting the Glazers to make haste back across the Atlantic.

The contradictions fizzed everywhere on this thick, still night. Earlier on Wednesday Carrick will doubtless have been spared the news that sacking season had already visited the Ineos football empire. At this point Jim Ratcliffe’s sporting citadels are more akin to a line of Dickensian rubbish heaps, their proprietor a modern-day golden dustman, and the plug had been pulled on Luka Elsner and United’s hapless junior sibling, Lausanne Sport. They are bottom of the Swiss top flight and results, a club statement explained, had been the determining factor in the manager’s demise.

They have not exactly helped Carrick either . Mainoo had claimed in a transactionally toned pre-match press conference that United could be “one win away” from changing the shape and scope of their season. In reality all that can be guaranteed about whatever occurs next is the sheer theatre of it. Of course it is Unai Emery, discussion whose suitability or otherwise for any United vacancy has brought surprising ramifications, who walks into this perplexing cocktail of loathing and unconditional support this weekend. Carrick will need the football to perform him a few more favours yet.

title: ‘I wasn’t performing’: Bruno Fernandes says Carrick was right to drop him after criticism
author: Nick Ames at Old Trafford
text:
‘If it was punishment for the words, it was right’

Carrick hails ‘magical’ Old Trafford after comeback win

Bruno Fernandes said Michael ­Carrick was correct to drop him last month as he reflected on a remarkable Manchester United comeback win against Roma at Old Trafford.

A twice-taken penalty from ­Fernandes set United’s revival from 2-0 down in motion, two goals from Matheus Cunha ultimately sealing a win that could yet save the embattled Carrick’s job.

Fernandes had been dropped after their previous Champions League game, a 4-1 humbling at Como , ­having criticised the manager’s ­tactics in a post-match interview. He was an unused substitute against Bournemouth in their next fixture and said he accepted the short-lived demotion.

“The manager took a decision of making myself on the bench because I wasn’t performing. And that’s fair,” Fernandes said. “Everyone felt like that was a punishment for the words that I had [after Como]. And if it was, it was right.

“The manager makes the ­decisions. I have to accept it. I have to go forward with that. It doesn’t change the belief I have in the manager, the staff and every player at this club. And it doesn’t change my aim to win every game that I have ahead of me.”

Fernandes attempted to take the attention away from Carrick after United’s first win in 10 games, which was sealed amid a raucous atmosphere pockmarked by protests against the club’s ownership. They narrowly avoided completing their longest winless run during a single season since March 1978.

“We don’t need to save anyone’s job,” he said. “The club needed that win. The players needed that win. It is something we needed as a group of players and staff. We have been working so hard to get out of this situation together.”

A satisfied Carrick hailed the magic of Old Trafford after United’s rip-roaring second half. “I don’t like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do in history and what’s gone before them too much, but it’s there,” he said. “This place does magical things, it’s done it before and it’ll do it over and over again at some point in the future. There’s just something in this place that when we do have these types of night, we do it the hard way.”

Carrick heaped praise on the 19-year-old substitute Shea Lacey, who brilliantly set up Cunha’s winner on his 10th senior appearance. “We love him to bits,” he said. “He’s a great young man, he’s desperate to do well, he’s got great ability. He’s got that little glint in his eye, he plays with a bit of mischief if you like.”

title: Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks
text:
Manchester United came from two goals down to beat Roma in a dramatic Champions League tie on Tuesday to give manager Michael Carrick a much-needed boost as he fights to save his job.

Things were looking bleak at Old Trafford when his side found themselves 2-0 down after just 17 minutes against their Italian visitors, who had not lost in their 10 Serie A games this season.

A nine-game winless run had left Carrick's position increasingly precarious and a poor start left United facing another damaging defeat.

But they stormed back in the second half with a show of character and class that had been missing in a troubled campaign where they had previously won just twice in all competitions.

Captain Bruno Fernandes started the fightback from the penalty spot before Matheus Cunha struck twice in the space of three memorable minutes to turn the game on its head.

What had threatened to be another night to forget became unforgettable for the Old Trafford faithful, while Carrick could breathe a little easier after his side pulled off an unlikely success.

United, though, are hardly the first side to snatch victory from the jaws of defeat on Europe's biggest stage.

Here are some of the greatest comebacks in Champions League history.

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

'We don't need to save anyone's job,' says Man Utd captain Fernandes

Tottenham travelled to Ajax for the second leg of their semi-final trailing 1-0, and things went from bad to worse in Amsterdam when Matthijs de Ligt and Hakim Ziyech put Ajax 3-0 ahead on aggregate before the break.

Spurs needed to score three times without reply to progress on away goals, and were given a glimmer of hope 10 minutes into the second half through Lucas Moura - and it was game on just four minutes later.

Moura pounced on a loose ball in the box after Fernando Llorente's shot was saved and he curled home to put the hosts on the ropes.

The stunning turnaround was completed in the 95th minute when Moura recorded a hat-trick to seal Tottenham's spot in the final on away goals, leaving Ajax players strewn across the turf in disbelief.

Just 24 hours before Tottenham's heroics in Amsterdam, Liverpool had overturned their own three-goal deficit.

The Reds' hopes of forcing their way back into the semi-final after a 3-0 loss to Barcelona at the Nou Camp looked slim, especially with Mohamed Salah and Roberto Firmino unavailable because of injury.

But Divock Origi got the ball rolling on seven minutes, before the tie really turned in the space of 166 seconds after half-time when substitute Georginio Wijnaldum scored twice.

A moment of quick thinking saw Liverpool complete the job as Trent Alexander-Arnold spotted Barcelona's defence switch off from a corner, whipping the ball in low for Origi to fire home and spark wild scenes at Anfield.

That iconic line from commentator Peter Drury summed up an incredible night as Roma clinched a memorable comeback to send Barcelona packing in the quarter-finals.

Own goals from Daniele de Rossi and Kostas Manolas helped Barca record a 4-1 win in the first leg at the Nou Camp.

Edin Dzeko's late goal in Spain gave Roma something to build from and the forward struck early in the return leg to further strengthen their belief.

De Rossi atoned for his own goal with a second-half strike and, with just eight minutes to go, Manolas headed home a corner to end Roma's 34-year wait for a place in the semi-finals of Europe's leading competition.

Arguably the greatest comeback of all, this one is so iconic that it has its very own title in France and Spain - La Remontada (The Comeback).

PSG were clinical at home, winning 4-0, but the Nou Camp sensed something special when Luis Suarez scored after just three minutes in the second leg.

Barcelona were two goals to the good at the break courtesy of a Layvin Kurzawa own goal, but still trailed by two goals on aggregate.

Lionel Messi scored a penalty soon after the restart but Edinson Cavani hit back to silence the home faithful, although it wasn't the pendulum-swinging moment PSG hoped for.

Barcelona, now trailing 5-3, needed three goals in fewer than 30 minutes to achieve a miracle. Neymar scored a free-kick in the 88th minute to offer further hope, before the Brazilian stroked home a 91st-minute penalty to level the tie at 5-5 on aggregate.

But PSG were still heading through on away goals.

Then, with 20 seconds of added time remaining, La Remontada came to fruition when Sergi Roberto turned home Neymar's chipped pass, with Barcelona becoming the only team in history to overturn a four-goal Champions League deficit.

Deportivo La Coruna, currently plying their trade in the second tier of Spanish football, are no longer associated with the Champions League - but they carried out an unforgettable fightback against heavyweight opposition in 2004.

Milan travelled to Spain with a 4-1 lead from the first leg, but Deportivo were not ready to roll over.

Walter Pandiani, who broke the deadlock at the San Siro, got the Spaniards up and running on home soil.

Unlike the first leg when they sat back after taking the lead, Deportivo threw caution to the wind and it paid off as they wiped out Milan's aggregate advantage in just 43 minutes after goals from Juan Carlos Valeron and Albert Luque.

That would have been enough for Deportivo to go through on away goals but they continued to press and Fran slotted home a fourth to confirm Carlo Ancelotti's side were heading out.

title: Manchester United produce comeback for the ages as Cunha double floors Roma
author: David Hytner at Old Trafford
text:
Michael Carrick enjoyed one of his finest nights as a Manchester United player in the Champions League against Roma, scoring twice in a 7-1 win in the quarter-final, second leg in 2007. The re-run here was all about his managerial survival at the club.

The situation looked impossibly grim for him at half-time. Amid an atmosphere of continued fan anger towards the United ownership, Carrick’s team had been implausibly bad. Roma took a 2-0 lead into the break and the truth was that the scoreline greatly flattered United.

What happened next was a fightback for the ages. For Carrick, it might even have topped 2007. United’s defending had been so loose, so generous. But they finally showed the other side to their game – the one about attacking punch; derring-do. They found a solution to their woes at the back. Keep the ball in the other half.

Matheus Cunha was the hero and it said plenty about the chaos of this game, the wildness of the emotions, that he ended up being sent off for a second yellow card in the 90th minute for a lunge at Leonardo Balerdi.

Before that, he had supplemented a Bruno Fernandes penalty – which the captain converted after a retake – with a touch and finish following an error from Balerdi. Cunha’s second goal, which proved to be the winner, was hammered in off the near post after a pass from the substitute, Shea Lacey. Cunha’s first touch to control was a beauty.

The United support sing about having seen it all. This was just extraordinary. Can it save Carrick? He will go into Sunday’s Premier League game at home against Aston Villa with renewed belief.

The fragility of the United backline has been well documented. How the hierarchy decided that it did not need any reinforcements over the summer is beyond belief. With Luke Shaw still injured, Carrick was forced to persist with Diogo Dalot out of position at left-back.

Dalot pushed very high at the outset, which felt bold. It was plainly a demand from Carrick. Dalot’s positioning was pure folly on the opening Roma goal. The visitors transitioned quickly, far too quickly for United’s ponderous defence and when Rodrigo Mora looked up from the inside left, all he could see was Matías Soulé in acres of space on the opposite channel. Where was Dalot? Mora played the pass. Soulé took a touch and swept past the exposed Senne Lammens.

United’s defending for the second goal was even worse. Leny Yoro turned and ran back towards his own goal as Roma advanced up the left, and when the move appeared to have broken down for them around the United box, there was Harry Maguire to gift it back to Soulé with a dreadful miskick. Soulé dropped his shoulder and shot; the ball hit Ayden Heaven’s hand and Donyell Malen converted from the spot. Again, Dalot had been high up the pitch.

The mutiny could be felt before kick-off; the sounds of it heard. There were the green and gold balloons of protest against the Glazers. The relentless chants against the club’s owners. When the clock showed 20 minutes and five seconds – or 2005; the year of the Glazer takeover – the Stretford End erupted in a planned move; hurling tennis balls down on to the pitch.

Moments earlier, a grisly Dalot error on the ball had almost led to Malen getting in for a third and the first half was just an ordeal for United. Roma were well organised in their 3-4-2-1 shape and they got in up the inside right time and again. They might have had many more before the interval; Mora, Malen and Soulé all went close.

United offered minimal resistance. They were so easy to play through. There was nervousness from them on the ball, heavy touches. A glaring lack of cohesion. What was the plan? When Bruno Fernandes had a half-chance on the edge of the box in the 43th minute, he could not sort out his feet and blazed high.

Carrick was in the last chance saloon during half-time. He had to have a simple demand of his players: show some fight. There had been no evidence of it in the first period. Yet United emerged with purpose.

Carrick lost Carlos Baleba in the 46th minute. The midfielder stormed into the Roma area and was about to shoot only to pull his hamstring. Then, United caught a break – two, actually – and the mood shifted sharply.

It was a soft penalty award for a push by Gianluca Mancini on Cunha after he played a give-and-go with Fernandes. But when United had that sinking feeling after Fernandes saw his kick saved by Devis Vásquez, they were reprieved when the referee, Jesús Gil Manzano, ordered a retake for encroachment. Fernandes lashed it home.

United came alive. Bryan Mbeumo, played through by Cunha for a one-on-one with Vásquez, saw his shot hit one post and then the other one before refusing to cross the line. United threatened from corners. Maguire went close. Dalot had a header cleared off the line.

The United support had endured that familiar wrestle before kick-off; trying to find hope in face of the negativity, the deep sense of foreboding. Kobbie Mainoo’s return to the starting XI provided a glimmer. He was in the mood to make his moves.

Carrick’s major selection decision was to start Heaven over Lisandro Martínez in central defence. It shone a light into Martínez’s current headspace. It is a dark place. Martínez would get on for Heaven towards the end.

United fought. It was shocking to see how Roma, unbeaten so far this season in Serie A, fell apart. Cunha made the difference. United deal only in the craziest of extremes.

title: Why Our Performance-Obsessed Editor is Willing to Give Up 3 Watts for Giant’s New Helmet
author: Josh Ross
text:
Breathability on par with vented helmets Visibility in an aero position Brow stays put when tightened Fidlock buckle

Lacking Virginia Tech Score Technically slower than other helmets

I am deeply interested in helmet aerodynamics for one simple reason: it is the cheapest wheel upgrade you can buy. While a lightweight, deep-section aero wheelset might cost upwards of $4,000, a high-end aero helmet normally costs in the $350 range but provides the same benefit. Going from shallow climbing wheels to deep aero wheels might save you about 10 watts, and that’s roughly the same as swapping your standard ventilated helmet for a fast aero road helmet. Go for both if you can, but if you have to pick one, it’s pretty obvious the helmet makes more sense.

More likely, though, in 2026, your bike already came with deep aero wheels and you still need a helmet. I always recommend picking an aero helmet for the free watts, but there are obviously other considerations. It has to keep you cool in the heat, it has to be safe, it has to be comfortable, and it has to look good.

After years of neglect, the Giant Pursuit got an unexpected update as we close in on the tail end of 2026. The tricky thing for every other helmet company right now is just how good the Specialized Evade 4—my current pick for best overall in the best bike helmets buyer’s guide —actually is. Because of that, I’ve almost started to expect less from other brands. Then the Giant Pursuit showed up, and I took it to Death Valley to ride in 30 mph winds and 109-degree temps. It was so good it was worth telling you about. Here’s why I am so impressed with the 2026 Giant Pursuit aero helmet.

Let’s clear up a lingering misconception: a modern aero helmet gives up nothing when it comes to ventilation. In 2026, brands use advanced internal channeling to capture air and pull it across your scalp as you move forward. When you slow down on a steep climb, it gets hot—but that is true whether your helmet is highly vented or completely solid. The Giant Pursuit is no different. I really did wear it in 109-degree heat through Death Valley. It was undoubtedly hot, but the more enclosed aero shell actually proved to be an advantage by keeping my scalp from getting sunburned.

Beyond the thermal management, my favorite feature of the Giant Pursuit is the field of vision in a deep aero tuck. With the Specialized Evade 4, as well as other options, I often struggle to get as low as I want while still seeing past the front brow of the helmet. Giant carved out just enough space at the front lip so you don’t have to crane your neck uncomfortably to see up the road.

Part of that is that the Pursuit also excels at stability. Over long miles, many helmets—aero or not—have a tendency to slowly slip down and rest against the top frame of my sunglasses. Giant designed a retention system that tightens down securely without creating pressure points on the forehead. It stays exactly where you put it, and the internal padding manages moisture well enough that when it finally saturates, the sweat drips clear of your lenses rather than blurring your vision.

This one is a little tricky, but what I ultimately don’t like is knowing this is not the absolute fastest helmet for me. I took a GiBLI G10 aero sensor out and tested this helmet directly against the Specialized Evade 4. Same day, same bike, same everything but the helmet. The difference was 3 watts at 25 mph, or 2 watts at 20 mph. I’m not going to sit here and say that’s a massive dealbreaker, but if I can pick between two good helmets and one is faster, why wouldn’t I? Ideally, the Pursuit would match the Evade 4’s speed while keeping that superior field of vision in an aero tuck. Perhaps that visibility is only possible because of the aerodynamic tradeoff, but I can wish.

I also wish we had a Virginia Tech test score. I suspect the helmet would do well simply because Mips-equipped helmets tend to score highly in the Virginia Tech testing protocol, but when you don’t have an answer, it remains an open question. For plenty of riders, that lack of third-party safety validation will be a far more serious issue than any potential wattage win or loss.

The main reason I wanted to write about the Pursuit helmet is essentially a livability detail, so I’ll say it again: the field of view in an aero tuck is excellent.

Beyond that, Giant is using a Fidlock buckle. I’ve included that in the pros, but that’s being very generous. It’s nice enough, but I’ve never once thought to myself that what I really needed was a magnetic buckle. It’s a solution to a problem that doesn’t exist.

On the other hand, the rear retention dial has gotten stuck once or twice and proven to be a little fiddly. For comparison, Specialized uses an FS2 BOA Fit System for the rear dial, and it’s excellent. Both Fidlock and BOA are third-party brands that require extra cash for inclusion. If I can only have one, I’d much rather see that budget spent on the BOA dial than the magnetic buckle. That said, none of this is a dealbreaker.

I recently ran a Velo Helmet Priority Poll asking what matters most when buying a helmet. Only 11 percent of respondents said their first priority is maximum aerodynamic performance and free watts. On the other hand, 45 percent said fit, comfort, and aesthetics are the ultimate deciding factors. You might think that means I suddenly have to back off aero as an important metric, but that’s not how I see it. The results actually make perfect sense to me, and it’s exactly how I would coach all aero-focused riders to think. Aero gains should never come at the cost of comfort. When an aero-focused product is designed right, that speed is an added benefit.…

title: Player Grades: Knicks 103, Nets 90
author: Russell Richardson
text:
Shamet and Hart score the highest marks, as the Knicks had the Nets their sixth loss of the season.

For three quarters Monday night, the Knicks looked like they might actually lose to the Nets. The Nets? The last place Nets? While we might get apoplectic, the champs seemed unconcerned about falling behind. When they finally flipped the switch, they turned a 79–75 deficit into a 103–90 win, outscoring Brooklyn 28–11 in the fourth at the Garden. That’s 15 straight wins against the neighbors. Landry Shamet did a lot of the work to make it so.

22 points (6–8 FG, 4–6 3PT, 6–6 FT), 1 rebound, 1 assist in 30 minutes

On a night when the starters happily hurled threes like pre-teens playing Pop Shot, Shamet sank a steady four of six, plus every free throw he took. His season-high 22 kept the Knicks in it long enough for the rest of them to wake up.

While the Knicks spun their wheels in third-quarter mud, Josh Hart collected his fourth foul with a lotta game remaining. Shamet replaced him at 8:44 and scored six points on perfect shooting from downtown. The first, at 2:26, cut Brooklyn’s lead to a single point; the second, with a minute left, made it 77-75. According to Basketball Reference, he had a team-high game score of 19.4. Pretty good for a sub.

8 points (3–6 FG, 2–5 3PT), 6 rebounds, 7 assists, 3 steals in 27 minutes (+22)

Hart had a crooked finger in just about everything that made the fourth quarter exciting. In that final frame, he hit a Kolek-assisted three to pull the Knicks within one, then assisted on back-to-back Anunoby threes and a Kolek layup (everybody seems to enjoy playing with Tyler, don’t they?). Josh intercepted a Julius Randle pass and took it the other way for a layup. His grade suffers for taking just six shots and collecting six fouls, but maybe he deserves a little more love for being a team high +22?

18 points (4–10 FG, 3–7 3PT, 7–8 FT), 4 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals in 38 minutes

OG played 38 minutes, got to the line eight times, and hit back-to-back threes in the fourth when the Knicks finally started to put Brooklyn away. Seven free throws will do a lot for a night when only four shots fall from the floor. Give credit to his stamina: after bumping bodies with that bull Julius Randle all night, he still had gas in the tank to help his team in the fourth. He hit the go-ahead three at 10:29 and another bomb 28 seconds later to make it 84–79. He also set up Clarkson’s transition three. Loses points for still struggling to finish at the rim.

11 points (4–11 FG, 1–4 3PT), 16 rebounds, 5 assists in 35 minutes

A weird game for Karl-Anthony. He had double-digit rebounds in the first half, but zero points. After intermission, he scraped together 11 points with much more aggressive drives to the rim. As New York rallied in the fourth, he banked in a short fadeaway, grabbed three defensive boards, and found Landry Shamet for the Knicks’ final basket. His back up, Andre Drummond, grabbed nine boards in his 13 minutes, but dividing the workload between the pair is unsustainable. James Wiseman is glued to the bench. Leon, what’s your move?

19 points (6–16 FG, 4–11 3PT, 3–6 FT), 2 rebounds, 6 assists in 33.5 minutes

Four threes and six assists are dandy, but missing half his free-throws and ten field goal attempts had us a little worried. He’s been mostly automatic since coming to New York, so forgive us for jumping to conclusions like: maybe he should spend less time doing extracurricular activities and more in the gym? He started off the game great, making 3-of-4 from deep, but then disappeared for a while.

7 points (3–5 FG, 1–2 3PT) in 11 minutes (+17)

Some guys can do a lot in 11 minutes. Clarkson squeezed seven points into his sliver of time (entirely in the second half) and was still a +17. As the fourth quarter started, a game that had been a nuisance all night was finally starting to break open. Jordan blocked Nolan Traoré’s layup and hit a transition three seven seconds later to push the lead to 10. He added a floater at 4:00 to keep the momentum going. He loses a point for collecting two fouls and a technical foul in the span of a minute during the third period, which didn’t help matters while the team was flailing.

After the game, coach Mike Brown offered high praise for the vet. “I’ve been around some good teammates when it comes to players. He’s gotta be the best. He’s the definition of ultimate pro,” he said. “You have a veteran that’s been there, done that, and he’s willing to accept the role that most guys wouldn’t accept […]. And he’s willing to accept it… and still try to uplift everybody and connect everybody while he’s going through what he’s going through. That’s the ultimate team player.”

6 points (2–4 FG, 2–4 3PT), 1 rebound, 2 assists in 16.5 minutes

Deuce hit two of four from deep and added a couple of assists. A decent shift on a night when the Knicks could’ve used a few more of those. Two steals is great. Four shots in almost 17 minutes seems insufficient, however.

6 points (1–7 FG, 0–2 3PT, 4–4 FT), 2 rebounds in 16 minutes (−11)

Hoo boy. Bridges made one shot from the floor and did little on defense to make up for it. The Knicks lost his 16 minutes by 11 points, the worst mark in the rotation. At least he got to the foul line for the first time after six games.

It’s perhaps too soon to sound the panic alarm, but he has shot 16 of 52 for the season. Mike Brown has taken notice. He ended Kal’s night after just a few minutes into the third quarter, and when he sent the starters back at the end of the game, Shamet took Bridges’ spot.

The Knicks got away with three quarters of sleepwalking because Shamet kept them close and Hart, OG, and the bench gave them life in the fourth. Next up are the Bulls on Wednesday. In their first meeting of the season, last week, the Knicks won but needed 48 points from the bench to bail them out. Do we see a trend emerging?

title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
text:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

The deal should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, £25 Phytosanitary certificates, inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees, sampling fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU.

UK exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes will also be able to resume.

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

It will also allow for passports for UK pets to be taken into the EU, while the UK will commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards. This process is called "dynamic alignment".

In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.

"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.

Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.

While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.

The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.

The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.

The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans .

A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.

Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.

While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.

But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".

At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".

"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."

The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.

The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

title: Eric Brunner finds his groove and 'a little bit of an adrenaline rush' with pair of wins ahead of Pan-American Cyclo-cross Championships
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
A total of 46 weeks have passed since Eric Brunner won his third US elite men's cyclo-cross championship, and only once, at the UCI World Cup in Benidorm, has he worn the stars-and-stripes jersey.

The 27-year-old focused on road racing this summer which delayed his return to cyclo-cross, but he made an emphatic arrival with back-to-back wins in UCI C2 races in Massachusetts over the weekend.

Brunner overcame crashes and flat tyres to win both rounds of the 35th Cycle-Smart Northampton Cyclocross, joined on Saturday's opener by his Competitive Edge Racing teammates on the podium - reigning Pan-Am champion Andrew Strohmeyer in second and Dylan Zakrajsek in third - who both have two months of racing in their legs.

The US champion said both days he used time trial mode - a discipline where he was best in stages at the Tucson Bicycle Classic, Redlands Bicycle Classic, third in Tour of the Gila, and sixth at the US Pro Road Nationals.

"This is my first race of the season, so I wanted to take it out a little conservatively and just see how I felt. Oftentimes, when I start going this hard for the first time, I get a little bit of an adrenaline rush and just feel a little weird. So, I just got in the group and found my groove, and found I felt pretty good," Brunner told organisers at the finish.

"It was more about just not making mistakes and capitalising if somebody else did. But, I bobbled one time and went down one time. I was just on my own for the last couple laps, and it was just a time trial to the finish. "

On Sunday, on a dry but technical Look Park course, Brunner recovered from two flat tyres, the second on the final lap, and held off Aidan Vollmuth (Donovan Racing) by 12 seconds for the victory. Luke Walter (CXD Trek Bikes) took third another 31 seconds back. Zakrajsek finished fourth while Strohmeyer had some challenges in a wooded section of the course to finish seventh.

"I got away early, but had a flat. There were a lot of roots and rocks out there, and I think I may have hit something. I hit my rims all day. I had another flat on the last lap, but thankfully by then I had enough of a gap it didn't matter that much," he said after Sunday's race, noting when he hit the front with four laps to go before drilling the pace solo.

In the elite women's races, New England native Lizzy Gunsalus (VIA LLP p/b Van Rysel) carried the Pan American champion's jersey to double victories at Northampton. The 23-year-old, who has been racing NoHo CX since she was 12 years old, won by two minutes on Saturday over Emma Betuel (DRRT) in second and third-placed Bridget Wilson another 24 seconds down.

On Sunday, she led start to finish with clean lines and a clean white Pan Am kit but had to hold off 19-year-old Lidia Cusack (CXD Trek Bikes), who finished 16 seconds back. The rest of the field was more than 2:45 back, with Daniela Bronk third and Ellen Noble fourth.

Like Brunner, Gunsalus filled her summer with road racing, competing for a fourth season with CCB p/b Levine Law Group, and earning a podium at Green Mountain stage race and the gold medal in the team time trial at the US Collegiate Road Nationals. Among her seven 'cross wins last year were championship titles in elite categories at Pan Ams and US nationals.

"Excited to have taken back to back wins at NoHo CX. Everything is dialed in and carrying good momentum into next weekend to try to defend my Pan-Am title," she wrote on Instagram.

The next races on the North American calendar are Pan-American Championships, taking place Saturday in Washington, D.C. , for a second consecutive year at the Armed Forces Retirement Home. Gunsalus faces stiff competition with three former elite winners in the field - Lauren Zoerner, Sidney McGill and Raylyn Nuss. And the entire podium from the U23 race are registered for the elite race this year - winner Mia Aseltine, Alyssa Sarkisov and Lidia Cusack.

The elite men's field at Pan Ams will most likely be a back-and-forth engagement between Brunner and Strohmeyer, who now ride for the same Comp Edge team. Brunner won the men's elite title at Pan Ams four consecutive times before being supplanted by Andrew Strohmeyer last year. However, neither was providing tips on how they would work together on Saturday.

"I couldn't ask for a better start to the season here. Usually the first race takes me a little bit to get going, so I'm really looking forward to Pan Ams," Brunner told organisers after his win on Sunday.

"I've just got a little bit of training this week but a lot of rest and I'll give it my best at Pan Ams."

title: Giro d'Italia boss says motor-racing circuit sprints will improve safety, but recent Tour de France evidence suggests otherwise
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
One of them, the iconic Monza track, will host the start of the all-important stage 15 time trial, but the other two – the Marco Simoncelli circuit on stage 4 and the Mugello circuit on stage 11 – are set to play host to big bunch sprint finishes.

This, said Guercilena, who took up his role as cycling director of RCS Sports following his departure as Lidl-Trek team manager this summer, was a deliberate ploy in the ever-more-urgent push for rider safety.

"The initiative stems from listening to athletes and teams regarding the need for safe finishes," he said on stage during the presentation of the route on Tuesday.

"This ties into the broader requirement for environments where even children can train securely. We believe that the Giro d’Italia, which also has a role in fostering cycling culture, can promote the use of motor racing circuits as new hubs for youth teams, allowing young riders to train in a safe setting. This offers families peace of mind, knowing their children can cycle in a secure environment.

"From a competitive standpoint, it also ensures that athletes have a very wide finish area, enabling them to perform at their best, and, above all, safely," he added.

The use of motor racing circuits, which have wide tracks and smooth surfaces, would intuitively appear to make sense when it comes to safety, avoiding the road furniture and pinch points associated with city-centre finishes on public roads.

However, the evidence – admittedly very limited – is not so supportive, with the last Grand Tour sprint finish on a motor track resulting in a slew of crashes and several riders airing safety concerns.

The 2023 Tour de France example

The first crash occurred on one of the straights with 1.7km to go, with a bump of shoulders sending multiple riders to the ground, including a stage favourite, Fabio Jakobsen. A second crash through a left-hand bend inside the final kilometre sent more sprawling and further fragmented the bunch, leaving only around 25 riders to play out the sprint. Another crash against the barriers in the full swing of the sprint capped off a finale that was remembered more for the spills and less for the thrills.

The crashes were not all necessarily linked to the fact this finale was taking place on a motor racing track, but there were interesting comments from several riders suggesting this might indeed have had something to do with it.

"A circuit is not safer than a road to finish, I can tell you this,” said Mathieu van der Poel, who provided the lead-out for the day’s winner, Jasper Philipsen. "It was really fast and the corners are quite difficult to judge in the bunch and you also have nowhere to go so I'm really happy I managed to stay upright."

"None of us are used to finishing on such a wide course, the entrance which is pretty small, then big lanes again. These kind of corners, everybody can keep pedalling and you can just take them 10 next to each other. In the end it’s like having a long straight but even more dangerous," he said.

"Sometimes people think the wider we make the roads and the more we go on circuits and whatever, the safer it becomes. But today we see the opposite. I think sometimes what makes it more safe is when you stretch out the bunch, like yesterday for example with the U-turn. Then the bunch gets stretched out, and from there on everybody keeps his position or kind of keeps his position, and then you get safer sprints."

It remains to be seen which exact sections of the two circuits are used at next year's Giro d'Italia, and crucially how many corners are involved, while various other factors naturally come into play as well – it's worth pointing out that some of that Tour de France chaos was attributed to the relative freshness after a very slow day until that finale.

But until everyone arrives safely and securely on stages 4 and 11, there might still be some holding of breath and some reserving of judgement when it comes to the suitability of motor tracks for cycling sprint finales.

What Makes This a Race Bike for Humans? Pivot Gets Into Road Bikes.
author: Will Tracy
text:
In this special episode of the Velo Podcast presented by Pivot, Chris Cocalis, Founder of Pivot Cycles, joins Mike Levy to discuss a new project from the Arizona, based brand.

Most people know Pivot for forward thinking mountain bikes, but now the brand is getting into road bikes with the Pravia, a bike Pivot is calling “a race bike built for humans.”

This is actually a return to road bikes for Pivot. The brand partnered with BH years ago on road bike product development and design from 2007 to 2012. Fast forward to today and Pivot has decided the time is right to get into this category under its own name.

“I just thought we could have a cutting edge product that was better,” said Cocalis.

For this project, he tapped into the innovative spirit at Pivot, like when the brand pushed into 29-inch wheels early, or developed a fat bike. “Pivot is our brand, and wherever we decide to take it we can compete in those categories,” he said.

Although there was some consideration for making a super lightweight, specialist bike, Cocalis really wanted to get back to having one good road bike to ride everything. So the Pivot team set forth to create the Pravia, a high-end road bike with elements that riders will find more comfortable, without sacrificing much in the way of performance. They have lovingly dubbed it “a race bike built for humans.”

Cocalis was deeply involved in the bike development process for the Pravia.

He walks us through the carbon layup development process. It took two years to get all the different sizes correct, and the 56 size around took at least six rounds of development to get the weight and ride quality where they wanted them. But it’s actually the smallest sizes that are the hardest to develop. Cocalis also talks to us about how Pivot’s Hollow Core Carbon Molding process for creating carbon frames differs from other brands. He calls it the most precise way to make a carbon frame.

Levy and Cocalis also get into the nitty gritty details that set this bike apart

Cocalis talked us through his decision to include downtube storage, a move that isn’t always perceived as being for performance bikes. It was also a massive development process to get a downtube storage door that “doesn’t squeak, doesn’t creak, doesn’t leak,” and that’s before trying to hit stiffness and weight targets. It’s part of the reason they needed six rounds of layup development on the size 56 frame alone.

Cocalis then discusses the decision to go all-in on electronic shifting. As he puts it, the Pravia is a high-end bike built for a rider that’s not interested in mechanical shifting. And making it electronic only means not sacrificing ride quality, performance, or weight to build in cable guides and stops. “It is definitely a performance minded decision,” Cocalis said.

Then there’s the small details that make the bike more livable, like a seatpost wedge that actually works—an apparently high bar to clear in this day and age.

Settle in for a great episode of the Velo Podcast!

Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
text:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.

Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.

Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".

In a post on X , external , Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.

These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.

Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.

It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.

The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.

The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.

Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened .

"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.

The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.

It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.

The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date .

US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.

The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.

Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday , denying it was behind the hack.

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.

The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.

The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .

Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X , external : "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."

As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.

It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

title: How sporting events are being affected by Middle East conflict
text:
The 2027 Asian Cup is just the latest event to be postponed in the Middle East amid concerns about missile attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement.

The 24-team tournament - Asia's version of the Euros - was scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia from 7 January to 5 February next year.

The Asian Cup has now been delayed by almost a year , and will be held between 23 December, 2027 and 21 January, 2028.

Sport in the region had already been heavily affected by the US-Iran conflict, which led to the cancellation of the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Formula 1 Grand Prix weekends in April this year.

Now the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi at the end of the year are also in doubt due to that ongoing situation and the current conflict involving the Houthis. If they are cancelled, F1 would have lost four of its 24 events this year.

It is not just football and F1 that have been forced to cancel, reschedule or move high-profile events, and many more remain under threat.

BBC Sport takes a look at the situation across the sports.

The Saudi Pro League has, for the most part, managed to carry on as usual.

Several ​domestic ⁠league games had to be postponed, including three fixtures last month as the situation escalated.

The games were moved in the immediate aftermath of the attack on a major airport in Riyadh - though the SPL said they were switched "as a result of mandatory minimum rest periods between matches and to accommodate logistical requirements".

Following the postponement of the Asian Cup, this weekend's full round of Saudi Pro League has been called off.

The league once again has not attributed this to conflict in the region, instead saying the calendar would be recalibrated after the cancellation of the Asian Cup to achieve "a more balanced distribution of fixtures".

The AFC Champions League has been affected as well.

Cristiano Ronaldo and Kingsley Coman were among Al-Nassr's star players who did not to fly to Uzbekistan this week "given the pressure of matches and the amount of travel involved".

Al-Wasl of the United Arab Emirates also opted not to fly to Saudi Arabia to play Al-Nassr, and the match will be rearranged.

Meanwhile, the wife of Ollie Watkins, who plays for Riyadh-based Al-Hilal, posted on TikTok that she would be staying in the UK with their two children "until it calms down".

"We've had a bit of a plot twist," said Ellie Watkins. "I have come back to the UK for a little bit.

"There's just a little bit of conflict and things going on over in Saudi and we basically decided just to stay here.

"I felt like I needed to do that for the kids so there is some form of normality until we can get back out there and all be together."

Other well-known stars playing in the country include Gabriel Martinelli, Tijjani Reijnders, Darwin Nunez, Ivan Toney, Alexandre Lacazette, Ruben Neves, Sadio Mane and Joao Felix.

Formula 1 has a major dilemma about racing in the Middle East both at the end of this season and the beginning of next.

Most pressingly, the 2026 season is due to end with races in Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

As things stand, the sport is pressing ahead with plans to go to those races after being given security reassurances from various governmental sources that it should be safe.

There are, though, many people within the sport with misgivings about going.

Should the situation in the Middle East deteriorate in the next week or so, they could be called off and replaced with a single event in Imola in Italy on the Abu Dhabi weekend.

The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, with Saudi Arabia hosting on the following weekend.

But as things stand between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthi separatists, that race could not go ahead, and is likely to be cancelled if nothing changes by December.

Bahrain and Saudi Arabia are linked by a causeway, at the Saudi end of which is a facility belonging to state oil company Aramco, which has been targeted by the Houthis, while it joins Bahrain close to the F1 track.

One option being discussed is to hold that race in Malaysia, as was done in October this year.

The Dakar Rally was due to take place in Saudi Arabia in January but has been moved "following recent developments in the region".

Now the 2027 edition will begin in Loule-Faro in Portugal and end in Marrakech in Morocco.

Saudi Arabia had hosted the previous seven editions of Dakar, and the intention is to return in 2028.

Rally Saudi Arabia, part of the 2026 FIA World Rally Championship, which was scheduled for 12–15 November, has been cancelled.

But MotoGP will still take place this weekend at the Lusail International Circuit in Doha, Qatar, with three races left in the season.

It will go ahead without the Yamaha team, which has been advised against travelling from Japan.

The Six Kings Slam, which should have begun on Saturday in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been postponed by two months.

It is now scheduled to run from 27 December to 30 December at the ANB Arena, located about 31km away from the King Khalid International Airport, which was the target of an attack on 10 October that killed 13 people and injured 308 others.

Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Alex de Minaur, Taylor Fritz and Learner Tien are due to compete.

But the 2026 WTA Finals, this weekend's season-ending championship of the women's tour, will not take place in Saudi Arabia.

A mutual agreement was reached to terminate a hosting agreement early, and it will instead take place at Indian Wells in the United States.

Saudi Arabia regularly hosts title fights and high-profile bouts.

Only last week, Mexican legend Canelo Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super middleweight championship against Christian Mbilli.

But the whole of the card did not survive as Lindolfo Delgado withdrew from his IBF lightweight title fight against Arthur Biyarslanov over safety concerns.…

title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’
author: Niha Masih
text:
A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

I t’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.

Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote , Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.

Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.

Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.

The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.

I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.

One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.

For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.

“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.

“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.

Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.

“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.

There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.

Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.

On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.

Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.

He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”

Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

title: Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
text:
Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain.

Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain.

Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice.

Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.

"By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said.

Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.

According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.

"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.

"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."

Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line.

But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.

title: Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
text:
Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.

The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.

While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.

Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.

The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.

Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.

"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."

The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.

In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.

If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.

The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.

A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.

The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.

Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.

There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.

Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.

He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

Giro d’Italia 2027 Route Reveal: Two Time Trials and Return of Zoncolan in Savage Final Week
author: ahood
text:
Monte Zoncolan returns to the Giro d’Italia in 2027 as the final exclamation point in a punishing third week that also packs in legendary climbs with a double ascent of the Mortirolo.

Organizers unveiled a challenging old-school course of 3,418.9km and 50,250m of climbing between the May 8 start in Trieste and the May 30 finish in the Italian capital, Rome.

The 110th edition of the corsa rosa will test the overall contenders, with two individual time trials totaling 56.9km, trademark early summit finishes, and an endless barrage of mountains following the second rest day across the Dolomites.

Will the course be tempting enough to attract the likes of defending champion Jonas Vingegaard or perhaps French ace Paul Seixas ?

The headline act is the return to Monte Zoncolan — the OG of cycling’s “impossible climbs” — for the first time since 2021. Riders will climb up the Ovaro approach, where Chris Froome won in 2018, on the Giro’s penultimate stage.

Before that comes an explosive day through the Alps, with the Mortirolo appearing twice along with the Gavia in a stage packing 5,700m of climbing in the Giro’s epic “queen stage.”

There is room for the fast men, too. Organizers circled six stages as sprint opportunities, alongside eight hilly stages, five mountaintop finales, and the two time trials.

The Giro opens with nine consecutive racing days and enough climbing to separate the pink jersey pretenders from the contenders.

Trieste hosts an opening stage that crosses into Slovenia and squeezes three challenging climbs into the final 40km. Stage 2 stays entirely in Slovenia, linking Ljubljana and Koper, before another demanding day from Cervignano to Possagno.

Who knows? Maybe Tadej Pogačar will show up to race.

The sprinters should get their first clear opening at Misano’s motor racing circuit on stage 4.

The GC battle clicks into gear early with stage 5, starting in Filottrano to honor Michele Scarponi 10 years after his death. The day’s 139km pack 3,300 meters of climbing.

The first of two TTs comes with the 19.6km run from Sulmona to an uphill finish at Campo di Giove.

Naples follows before the opening Sunday brings another summit finish at Monte Livata.

The second week serves up plenty of asphalt to attack before the race reaches the brutal mountains looming in the north.

Racing resumes with 218km from Palombara Sabina to Norcia, where repeated climbs and descents totaling 3,600m sets the tone for week 2 packed with potential ambush country.

The race’s longest stage follows, finishing at the Mugello Circuit in a likely opportunity for the sprinters.

Tuscany then hosts the Tappa Bartali from Montecatini Terme to Zeri, featuring Passo dei Due Santi and a new uphill finish. A flatter run into Reggio Emilia offers some relief before a demanding weekend.

Saturday’s 187-kilometer stage to Piani di Bobbio/Valtorta gets heavy with 4,900m of climbing. The Ghisallo, Culmine di San Pietro, Miragolo San Salvatore, and Alino precede the uphill finale.

The week closes with the 37.3km individual time trial starts inside Monza’s racing circuit and finishes in Milan. The flat but technical route will favor the specialists and pressure the pure climbers to limit the losses.

The Giro comes out swinging for a brutal, old-school third week.

Coming a day after the rest day, stage 16 from Sondrio to Aprica could blow up the race at 192km and 5,700m of climbing. The stage features two ascents of the Mortirolo with the feared Gavia packed in between. The Gavia carries Cima Coppi honors as the Giro’s highest point, while the Mortirolo is the designated Montagna Pantani.

The sprinters get another chance from Chiari to Vo’ before the mountains return on the road from Rovereto to Madonna di Campiglio. Rovereto to Sacile, featuring 3,000m of climbing in 199km is perfect for the breakaways.

Then comes the return of Monte Zoncolan. The penultimate stage starts in Pordenone and finishes up the steeper Ovaro face in the final chance to crack the race wide open.

Rome is back for the final stage to pop the champagne after one last bunch kick.

title: Zwift Rider Spots ‘A Guy Taking a Dump’ in New Real-World Video Package
author: Jim Cotton
text:
One Zwift user got more than they were bargaining for when they took the platform’s new “real life” video format for a spin.

Sam Sky was virtually grinding along the Colorado River Sunrise highway on his indoor trainer when he spotted someone in the corner of his screen, crouched in bushes in the lay-by.

There was only one thing they could reasonably be doing: “Taking a dump.”

Sky grabbed a screencap of this surprise addition to Zwift’s new “Plus” package and shared it to the Zwift Ride Owners Group on Facebook.

“Zoom in on the green circle. I saw a guy taking a dump by the side of the road during my session this morning on the new videos,” Sky wrote Monday in the text accompanying his post.

And indeed, if you zoom in close enough, Sky doesn’t seem to be mistaken.

A figure with a white top can be seen hunched over, seemingly pushing their own take of Zone 2 into some scrubby foliage.

The post’s comments section inevitably lit up. Bad jokes about Tom Dumoulin mingled with snarky comments that Sky wasn’t training hard enough.

Zwift rolled out its “Plus” premium tier last week to a wave of hype.

The online training and racing giant added real-world video routes and adaptive coaching to a costly subscription model it considered a milestone.

For the first time, Zwifters could ascend iconic real-world climbs and zoom along touristic coastal roads rather than take on another rep of Watopia’s “Epic KoM.”

Excited early adopters like Sky likely didn’t expect Zwift’s expansion into the real world to be quite this realistic, however.

But fear not, Zwift is clearing up the mess.

A spokesperson told Road.CC on Tuesday that they’re working to scrub this unfortunate addition from its new premium package.

“We’re aware that the screenshot has been shared,” Zwift told Road.CC . “This is being addressed today. I’m sure that some readers may be slightly disappointed.”

title: 'Too ambitious in too many segments' – Bianchi to renegotiate debt repayments amid financial woes
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Italian bike manufacturer Bianchi has until late May to renegotiate payments of its debts amid a structural reorganisation after the company accrued huge debts.

According to a report by Bianchi has entered into 'Composizione Negoziata della Crisi' (CNC) on September 30, a court-backed status in Italy which means the company can delay paying its debts for a limited period and is intended to help businesses navigate financial problems.

This status applies to the brand's holding company, FIVE Bianchi SpA, from September 30 and lasts for four months from the date it was granted, though it an be extended to 240 days, which would give Bianchi until May 28 to renegotiate payments.

According to the report, Bianchi's most recent published accounts, released in late 2024, show that the brand owed €100 million, a large proportion of that to banks.

Should a solution to the company's crisis not be found by May, insolvency proceedings could then follow.

Since 1997 Bianchi has been owned by Swedish company Grimaldi Industri, which saw the company through the cycling boom which accompanied the Covid-19 pandemic. As the market contracted afterwards, however, the company continued to invest, introducing new bikes and opening a new factory outside Milan, which it hoped would build up to 1,000 bikes a day. This investment in a shrinking market saw it move inexorably from profit to loss.

This aggressive policy was accompanied by a flurry of Chief Executive Officers, with four joining the company since 2021. The latest of those is Tony Grimaldi, son of the parent company’s owner Salvatore Grimaldi, who was appointed in early summer as part of the restructuring plan.

"We were investing a lot in too many areas at the same time. We have been too ambitious in too many segments, and the bicycle industry is so tough," Grimaldi told . "You cannot do everything everywhere, especially when we know that the market is oversupplied.

"It's a structured way to be transparent that you are reorganising and restructuring," Grimaldi said, adding that the company is already in constructive talks with the banks.

Bianchi is one of the world’s oldest bicycle makers, opening for business in Milan in 1885 and with its trademark celeste colour scheme has become one of the sport’s most storied brands, sponsoring WorldTour teams until as recently as this year. However, last week WorldTour team Bahrain Victorious announced an end to their partnership with Bianchi, the team moving to Factor Bikes from next season.
