title: Giro d'Italia 2027 route – A comprehensive guide to all 21 stages
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
: 3,418.9 kilometres

: May 8, 2027 - May 30, 2027

With seven summit finishes, plenty of punchy terrain, and some brutal high-mountain stages particularly in the final week, not to mention one of the race's two time trials being uphill, the 2027 Giro certainly leans towards the climbing specialists.

It all kicks off on Trieste on May 8, 2027, and finishes in Rome on May 30, covering 3,418.9 kilometres and taking in 50,250 metres of elevation gain in total.

Here, we go through the route stage-by-stage to see what's in store for the pink jersey hopefuls next May.

The first pink jersey looks to be going the way of a puncheur, with an opening stage that ventures over the Slovenian border and features three short climbs in the final 40km, plus a downhill run to the line. It should be an explosive and exciting start to the race.

After the stage 1 foray, stage 2 takes place entirely in Slovenia, and it's another punchy one, with a short sharp climb topping out just 3km from the line and followed by a fast dip down into Koper. Attacks will fly.

A third successive stage that suits puncheurs and aggressive riders, with two modest categorised climbs and a false flat drag towards the finish another chance for the attackers to get rid of the sprinters.

The pure sprinters finally get their chance on stage 4, with very few complications on the run from Argenta towards the Marco Simoncelli motor racing track, where the sprint will be contested.

The proper climbing action comes early, with a first summit finish on stage 5. The organisers have only given this a three-star difficulty rating but the final climb to Sarnano-Sasotetto measures 13.1km at an average gradient of 7.4% and maximum pitches of 14%. It's a rude awakening and will provide an early indication of who's where in the fight for pink.

Stage 6 is another stage that could see a sprint, or could something a bit more dramatic, with 1,700 metres of elevation gain on a route that climbs steadily for the final 10km.

The second big general classification test of the 2027 Giro comes with the first of the two time trials, this measuring 19.6km but crucially heading uphill for pretty much the whole thing. The categorised part of the climb to Campo di Giove measures 12.5km at a modest average gradient of 4.4% but there are pitches of up to 9%. It's not quite a pure mountain time trial but it's far from a flat one and should provide an interesting test between the pure time trial specialists and the climbers.

Napoli is most openly associated with sprints, and we should see another one again here, though the undulating terrain in the finale and the rise to the line make it one for the lighter and more versatile of fast men.

An action-packed opening week closes with a second summit finish and third obvious GC flashpoint. The final climb of Monte Livata measures 13.9km at an average of 6.9%. Bigger mountain stages follow later in the race but by this point, after the time trial, things will be taking some sort of shape, and the favourites will surely hit out against each other towards the top of the climb.

The second week opens with an interesting stage that features a tricky pair of climbs in the finale and a fast descent to the finish in Norcia. It looks like prime terrain for a breakaway.

Another sprint stage with a complication. Some teams may look to use that late climb of Vetta Le Croci to drop the pure sprinters, but they have just under 30km to get back in to try and contest the victory, on another motor racing circuit.

Our third summit finish of the Giro takes us up the Passo Due Santi, a short one at 8.7km but viciously steep at an average of 8.7% with pitches well in the double digits. We're not expecting huge gaps but it's an important test where any weakness can actually be punished heavily.

There's still a climb in there, but finally, something pretty much nailed on for the pure sprinters, so expect a drag race in Reggio Emilia.

We've already had plenty of summit finishes but stage 14 marks the heaviest climbing stage so far, with 4,900 metres of elevation in this route that sets out from the Lombardy region and heads over the Madonna del Ghisallo climb used in Il Lombardia. Three further ascents follow before the final climb up the Piani di Bobbio, which measures 10.1km at an average of 9%. That's brutal, and coming at the end of a heavy climbing day, it's a huge day for the general classification contenders.

The second week closes with another huge test for the pink jersey hopefuls, in the form of the race's second time trial. Unlike the first, this is pan-flat, from Monza to Milan, and pretty long at 37.3km. It's one for the pure TT specialists, and one where the weaker of the GC contenders against the clock could take some pretty heavy blows from a time-loss point of view.

The final week opens with one of the hardest Grand Tour stages we've ever seen. There are 5,700 metres of elevation on this brute, which is extraordinary. What we have is a sandwich of Giro icons, with a double ascent of the mighty Mortirolo either side of a first trip up the Gavia since 2014. The Mortirolo has seen some historic Giro moments over the decades, with savage gradients, while the Gavia takes the riders up into the snowline at 2,600 metres of altitude – it's the 'Cima Coppi' as the highest point of the Giro. The final climb to Aprica is more of a drag but by that point the race will be in pieces and riders will be only be dragging their weary bodies towards the line. A monstrous day.

After that mountain monster, we pick up the theme of the opening days with a largely flat stage that throws a couple of short climbs into the finale – perfect launchpads for late attacks.

The second of three big mountain stages in the final week, this one features 4,500 metres of elevation over the course of five big climbs. The final climb to Madonna di Campiglio, at 12.5km and 5.7%, is not super difficult, but it's what comes before that matters, and that will drain the legs well in advance. This looks like one of those classic Giro mountain stages where there's a huge fight for the breakaway and chaos ensues for basically the whole day.

Another interruption to the climbing-fest in the form of yet another largely flat but still punchy day of racing. At this point, how many sprint teams will be left, and how much strength will be left? Stages like these so late in a Grand Tour are often ripe for breakaway action.

The Giro d'Italia will be decided at the summit of the Zoncolan, a beastly climb measuring 10.1km at a barely believable average gradient of 11.9%. It's fairly new to the Giro, with no visits before the 21st century, but it's becoming one of the race's icons, and is certainly in a bracket with the Angliru as one of the hardest climbs in professional cycling. With 3,600 metres of elevation, this stage is the lightest of the final week's mountains stages on paper, but this final climb overcomes those statistics on its own, to make this a pivotal – and final – juncture in the battle for the pink jersey.

The 2027 Giro concludes with a short stage in Rome made up of laps of a circuit through the Italian capital. Whatever sprinters are still standing will have the chance to fight for the final stage win before the overall champion is crowned.

text:
There's plenty of climbing in the 2027 edition of Giro Women. (Photo: Getty Images/RCS Sport)

The 2027 Giro d’Italia Women starts by the beach, but anyone chasing pink better bring their climbing legs.

Defending champion Demi Vollering will have her hands full, if she decides to return next season .

Running May 29 to June 6, the race covers 1,132km and packs in 17,450m of climbing between the seaside start in Viareggio and the mountainous finale in the Aosta Valley.

That is plenty of vertical packed into nine days for the season’s first women’s grand tour after La Vuelta Femenina is moved to October.

title: Giro d'Italia 2027 route revealed – A climber's paradise with double Mortirolo ascent and return to iconic Monte Zoncolan and Passo Gavia
author: James Moultrie
text:
The route for the 2027 Giro d'Italia has been revealed as a climber's paradise, with three of Italy's most difficult and iconic ascents set to feature as the highlights in May next year: Passo del Mortirolo (twice), Passo Gavia, and Monte Zoncolan.

At the presentation in Rome on Tuesday, race organisers RCS unveiled the 3,418km route from Trieste, near the Slovenian border, to Rome, with a major focus on the north of Italy, two individual time trials, and some days on offer for the sprinters and breakaway experts.

After two years of foreign starts, the returning to Italy will see racing kick off on Saturday, May 8, with two rest days breaking up the 21 stages and 50,250m of elevation gain before the finale on Sunday, May 30.

The real showpieces of the route will be the mountain stages, with the first return to the 2,600m-high Gavia since 2014 being sandwiched between a double ascent of the brutal Mortirolo on the queen stage 16, finishing in Aprica.

There are seven summit finishes in total, ranging in difficulty across the Apennines and Alps, with the GC also set to be shaken up by two time trials – one being a mountain race against the clock to Campo di Giove, and the other taking in the Monza motor racing circuit on a flatter test.

10 years on from Tom Dumoulin's maiden Grand Tour triumph at the Giro, this opens the door to a time trial specialist potentially dominating the road to Rome, though those aforementioned mountains will bring only the most complete riders to the fore in contention for the .

With the duo of time trials, RCS will be hoping to attract the likes of Remco Evenepoel as the leading star, with defending champion Jonas Vingegaard not expected to return, and 2024 winner Tadej Pogačar likely to opt for the Tour de France and Vuelta a España in 2027. Though the Belgian is all but certain to return to the Tour, a combination may not fit with his team's plans, so the organisers may have to look elsewhere for their headline name on the start list.

For those not chasing the iconic pink jersey, there will be between six and eight possible opportunities, though the pure sprinters see their chances squeezed as several uphill kicks and stages featuring late climbs offer up ground for opportunistic attackers or breakaway hunters to make their moves. All in all, it's a typical Giro route with something for everyone, albeit the first one not designed by Mauro Vegni – the previous race director who retired last year.

In an ideal world, organisers RCS would have hoped that a Grande Partenza in Trieste and early foray across the Slovenian border would've attracted the likes of 2023 winner Primož Roglič and 2024 champion Pogačar. However, with the former still having not signed for a new team for 2027 and the latter wanting to complete the Grand Tour set with the Vuelta, neither look like probable starters for May.

That being said, several of the world's best riders will descend on the northeast corner of Italy in Friuli-Venezia Giulia for the first Grand Tour of 2027, where the chaos, unpredictable weather, and brutal climbing of the Giro will be back at its best for the 110th edition.

The first pink jersey will be decided in Trieste on a punchy , where three short hills in the final 30km should pit the top puncheurs against the versatile sprinters, with the GC favourites just trying to stay out of trouble and potentially fight out a small group sprint.

will be battled out entirely in Slovenia from the capital city in Ljubljana to Koper, with another undulating route opening the door to the same types of riders who starred on stage 1. The same can be said of , when racing returns fully to Italy for a gradually rising uphill run to the line in Possagno in the Veneto region – again the puncheurs should have their day.

Following a longer transfer down to Argenta in Emilia-Romagna, the sprinters will have their first guaranteed opportunity of the 2027 Giro on , finishing at the MotoGP circuit, Autodromo Marco Simoncelli in Misano, near the Adriatic coast.

The first mountain top finish of the race arrives a day later on stage 5 to Sarnano Sassotetto, where the initial movements in the GC race will be made on the 13.1km ascent which averages 7.4% gradient. Only ranked with three stars of difficulty by the organisers, it's more of a GC loosener than a decisive day, with significantly easier climbs approaching the finale in the Marche region, but it will indicate who has survived the initial salvoes best in the fight for pink.

fits into the same category as the opening three days of racing, where a breakaway could easily jump up the road to fight it out on the east coast from Alba Adriatica to Lanciano, where undulating and dragging roads will lead to the finish.

The GC favourites will be looking to survive that ahead of the first really crucial day in the overall race. On , the action is the mountain individual time trial from Sulmona to Campo di Giove, where19.6km of racing and a testing 12.5km should completely reshuffle the standings and potentially the pink jersey holder. It's the first mountain ITT at the Giro since the race was decided on the penultimate day in favour of Roglič in 2023, but at just a 4.4% average gradient on the climb – which is almost 5km longer – it isn't as vicious as the 11.2% average from three years ago.

brings the 2027 Giro back to Naples for the sixth season in a row, and while it has typically been a sprint stage in that time, the profile points to more of a punchy finale, with several short kickers in the final 30km.

The first week comes to a close with the second summit finish of the race, albeit on a mountainous with just over 3000m of elevation gain. After a flat opening 70km, the stage win will be battled out to Monte Livata (13.9km at 6.9%), where the hardest gradients are all packed into the first 4km of the climb – it hasn't featured in the Giro before, but was used in the U23 men's Giro last season, where eventual winner Lorenzo Finn won solo by 52 seconds.

Monza time trial sets up final week

After the first rest day, the Giro gets back underway with two chances for the breakaway on and , the former finishing with two climbs in the last 30km and a long downhill run to the line, and the latter would be a certain sprint stage, if not for a final short sharp climb arriving with 28km to go.

It doesn't take long for GC action to resume with another summit finish on , as the race heads through its one and only stage in Tuscany towards the Passo due Santi on the border with Emilia-Romagna. It's 8.7km at 8.3%, and could prove the next major point in the fight, with the final 2.4km to the summit averaging more than 11% in gradient.

to Reggio Emilia is one of the almost guaranteed sprint stages, but the focus will quickly turn to those chasing the overall in Italy after a long transfer north into Lombrady. will he the hardest stage of the race so far when it arrives, taking the riders across just under 5000m of elevation gain en route to Piani di Bobbio. Four shorter climbs will precede the final 10.1km ascent which averages 9% gradient – a true brute in the Bergamasque Prealps, where if someone doesn't already have a commanding lead, this will be the best chance to take control yet.

The second week concludes with the second individual time trial of the race, a 37.3km pancake flat race against the clock on from the Monza F1 circuit to Milan. If Evenepoel isn't present, then it should emerge as a day for the likes of Filippo Ganna, where all the GC hopefuls will need to have recovered from the day prior's big mountain test.

Mortirolo double and Zoncolan to decide pink

In typical Giro fashion, the hardest stages of the 110th edition are all backloaded into the final week, and there is no such thing as a slow restart from the second rest day here, heading straight for the queen on Tuesday, May 25, from Sondrio to Aprica.

192km in length, with 5,700m of elevation gain, and featuring some of the most feared ascents in the Italian Alps, the organisers have opened the door to the race being completely flipped on its head with the Passo del Mortirolo being tackled twice in the same stage, with a return to the Passo Gavia sandwiched between the double header.

At 12.8km and averaging 10.1% gradients, the Mortirolo is a true icon of the Giro, but after the first time up, the riders won't have any respite as they descend back to the valley and begin the climb to the Gavia – a 16.5km brute with a more regular average gradient of 8%, but one which ventures to 2,600m in altitude. Following that with another rep up the Mortirolo and then a final climb to Aprica should make it one of the hardest races of the entire season, and where pink could be decided once and for all.

If, and only if, the sprinters have survived this long, they could be rewarded by a sprint into Vó, but two late hills in the last 20km could complicate that, and after such a brutal mountain stage, the breakaway hopefuls may be more likely.

With the legs still screaming from two days prior, the GC riders will have to go again on with a 4,450m elevation gain day to another summit finish at Madonna di Campiglio, but not before taking on the Passo Ballno, Passo Durone (twice), and Passo Daone. This final climb is much shallower at 5.7% average, so may be one for a break to get up the road as the GC favourites await the Zoncolan.

should see the sprint teams come to the fore again, but early climbs heading out of Rovereto will give a strong break an opportunity to form – but the fast men will have been so starved of opportunities at this point that staying away could prove very challenging.

The last time Monte Zoncolan characterised a route of the Giro d'Italia, it was barely seen in all its glory, with a foggy and cold day in 2021 being captured by Lorenzo Fortunato. The penultimate day of the race on will give someone a chance to join him, Chris Froome, and Michael Rogers as modern winners on this iconic mountain in the Carnic Alps. With the race returning to where it started in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region, the 10.1km climb at 11.9% average gradient should provide one final chance to capture pink, or to reaffirm dominance on a backloaded final mountain stage, with 3,600m of elevation gain packed into the final 50km of the route.

Whoever is in pink at the summit will be crowned the winner of the 2027 Giro d'Italia, with only the processional sprint circuit in Rome left to be completed on after a long transfer south to the capital.

Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
text:
Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.

Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme.

That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year.

But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit.

The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.

Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice.

"Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means."

The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.

But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold.

They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.

Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year

Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced.

With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost.

Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait".

"By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson.

"Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them."

The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks".

But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer.

The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers , external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.

It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed.

The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes:

Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller

Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more

Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman

The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty."

But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered.

"These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said.

The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February.

Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed". Three lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance - are also challenging the scheme.

The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled from 16 February to 3 March.

Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained can still complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free , external .

title: Shimano Dura Ace C50 wheel review: Rock solid all-round performance and the update the flagship wheelset needed
author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
text:
$2,970 / £2,298.99 / €2699.98

1318 grams - F: 600 R: 718 (with tubeless tape)

Internal - 23mm / External- 31 mm front / 32mm rear.

21 front and rear.

Shimano launched its new R9300 Dura-Ace wheel range in late July after months of under-the-radar pro-use shots and speculation.

I’d followed the wheels since the early spring, when we regularly saw Mathieu van der Poel racing on plain rims and hubs stamped ‘prototype’ .

Three days after Van der Poel’s magnificent win on the wheels in the final stage of this year's Tour de France, they arrived to market as part of an updated six-model range .

The C50 has long been the most commonly used Dura-Ace wheel; as the range’s all-rounder, it’s the one that tends to be raced on the most. Its 50mm depth makes it likely the fastest across the widest range of terrain.

The previous R9200 Dura-Ace wheels certainly weren’t boring, but it didn’t feel like they were many regular riders' first choice when it came to the best road bike wheels . I certainly didn't see many at all in the wild, and it's safe to say Shimano wheels are not as popular as their groupsets are.

Alpecin-Premier Tech were the single team riding the wheels in the men’s WorldTour, and the fairly standard (by 2026 wheels) steel spokes, low-key Dura-Ace graphics and rim profiles were possibly just a little underwhelming.

The new R9300’s seem to have been met with a positive reception all round, and their updated aesthetics have surely done some good.

I’ve been using the wheels for months to see how they perform and how they are to live with. Big logos and carbon spokes might have been two of the best things Shimano could have done visually, but what about the rest of the package?

Let’s start with what changed from the previous-gen R9200 wheels. The standout feature is the addition of Vonoa carbon fibre bladed spokes instead of steel ones.

The spoke count has also decreased from 24 to 21 spokes front and rear to save weight. The spoke nipples themselves are still external.

Carbon spokes aren’t automatically guaranteed to produce a good wheelset, but the weight savings and potential improved stiffness (depending on spoke count) that they provide are hard to ignore in a performance road wheel.

On the topic of weight, the new C50's weigh in at 1318 grams on my scales with tubeless tape. A much more competitive weight than the previous wheelsets' 1461-odd grams.

The rims themselves have also received an update; inner and outer widths grew to 23mm internal from 21mm. The external width is also now front- and rear-specific. The front rim is now 31mm wide, and the rear is 32mm. The wheels are optimised for 28-30mm tyres.

Shimano is also said to have tweaked the layup of the rim, essentially to help produce the best overall performance for a rim of this depth. Dura-Ace is equipment designed for racing, so that means sprinting, hard cornering, changes of direction and the like.

The wheels didn’t arrive with in-depth aerodynamic test data, though Shimano did cite a 2.7-watt aero drag saving at 48 km/h with 30mm tyres at the time of launch.

We haven’t taken the R9300 C50’s to the wind tunnel for our own CN Labs wind tunnel testing yet, but we will try to get some data for them in the future. The previous-generation C50's finished at the bottom end of the table when we last took them to the tunnel in 2024.

Dura-Ace hubs have long been viewed as precision, high-quality options, and notably the brand has stuck with a ‘cup and cone’, or loose ball bearing arrangement in its hubs, whereby the ball bearings sit in an open cage.

Whilst the hubs use open caged bearings, sealed cartridge bearings can still be found in the freehub body.

The brand believes that a cup and cone system provides advantages over a sealed cartridge bearing; this caged bearing arrangement incidentally is what Shimano's long-time rivals Campagnolo also use in its Record hubs.

The R9300 hubs now have replaceable bearing cups, making pretty much the entire hub assembly replaceable if needed. I’ve worked on Dura-Ace hubs where pitted and worn bearing cups meant essentially permanently compromised performance (new bearings and/or cones would prematurely wear in rough, worn cups); this should now be a thing of the past for customers if it gets to that point.

The hubs themselves are a classic Dura-Ace gunmetal grey, and have a big vertical wordmark on the shell. The end caps need cone spanners for removal; they don't just pull off.

The freehub body is aluminium like the outgoing generation and has a 3.5 degree engagement angle which gives 103 points of engagement. The freehub body currently accepts a regular Shimano 12-speed cassette; we understand that when it arrives, the new Dura-Ace groupset will use 13 sprockets. This makes me think those 13 sprockets will fill the same amount of space as 12. I can't see Shimano rolling out some sort of updated freehub body for already launched wheels.

Aesthetically, the combination of those bladed carbon spokes, matte rims, and a prominent ‘Dura-Ace’ logo on each side of the rim has really helped update the wheels' look and ‘coolness ’, in my opinion. In short, it strikes me as just what they needed.

These are Shimano’s all-rounders, and I can report that the C50’s offer strong performance no matter what you are doing. I’ve done various training sessions, general Zone 2 rides and hard chaingangs on them, including flat-out max sprints, and they handle it all with ease.

I set the wheels up tubeless with some 28mm Pirelli (deep breath) P Zero Race TLR SL-R tyres, for a full factory Alpecin-Premier Tech spec.

The tubeless setup was very easy to do with a track pump, which I find is now the norm for modern road wheels and tyres. The tyres have held air well, with some normal drops in pressure but no leaks or seepage. The factory Shimano tubeless tape install was also, as you might expect, very tidy.

The wheels' freehub is also quieter than most; there’s a recording below for you to listen to. It's actually a lot quieter than that in use. I’m a fan of a quiet freehub, but it’s down to user preference.

Regarding performance, the C50 wheels haven't blown me away in any one key area. They don't feel hyper stiff or super fast; they are just rock solid across the board.

Whether I've been out of the saddle climbing a double-digit gradient, sprinting flat out at the end of the club run, hunkered down and cracking on on the flat, or leaning them into fast corners, the C50's have handled everything without breaking a sweat. They feel fast and exciting to use, and for me, look very smart.

They don't feel quite as stiff and taught as the Vision Metron RS wheels I tested last year, but out-of-the-saddle lateral stiffness, handling characteristics, and slow-speed acceleration are all good.

Mid- to high-end road wheelsets are getting lighter and lighter, and I think the market is setting a standard for wheels to come with carbon spokes right now. The weight drop the Vonoa carbon spokes have helped provide is useful here, and helps the wheels feel light and zippy in use.

On some rough tarmac, the wheels have felt slightly harsh at times with 28mm tyres; the remedy is going up in tyre size and down in pressure. A 30mm may well be the optimal choice for anything other than very smooth tarmac, but for me they didn't quite have the same luxurious ride quality as the Roval Rapide CLX III wheels .

It's worth mentioning axle and bearing 'feel': the cup and cone system doesn't have quite the same buttery smooth, effortless feel as a quality sealed bearing. It's not bad, just different, and the wheels still spin very well.

If you are buying a set, I’d recommend at least a yearly hub service. The best bet in the UK is to find and use an official Shimano service centre, where they should do things the right way, using the correct Shimano grease, etc.; these are top-end wheels and should be treated as such.

These wheels have an RRP of $2,970 / £2,298.99 / €2,699.98.

Expensive, but not as earth-shattering as some other top-tier models on the market; I think things could have been worse.

For a quick comparison, the recently launched Zipp 202 NSW wheels are very pricey at £3.400/$4,200/€3,800, the DT Swiss ARC 1100 wheels I tested earlier in the year are $3,218 / €2,499 / £2,599.98 with tyres and tubes included and the Roval Rapide CLX III's are $3,399.98 / £2,999.98 / €3,498.

Cheaper than some big-name competition, with solid performance and easily available spare parts.

This is a good update for the Dura-Ace C50 wheelset.

They haven't provided standout performance in one key area; they aren't the stiffest or the lightest out there. We also hope to gain our own wind tunnel test results for them in time to see how they fare against the competition.

What they are undoubtedly is a quality wheelset worthy of the Dura-Ace name. The C50's are all-rounders, and that is what you are getting with these wheels: solid performance across the board, in a more attractive overall package.

I'm expecting to see a few more pairs of these wheels out in the wild.

Testing scorecard and notes Solid overall design in line with the Dura-Ace name. Replaceable cups is a nice touch. A much needed aesthetics boost too.

Solid everywhere, not the strongest in one key area. Just great all rounders.

Now a lot more competitive at 1318 including rim tape. Good for a 50mm rim and sensible specs.

Very good, nice factory tubeless tape setup and all setups achieved with a track pump first time.

Cheaper than some competitors from Zipp, DT Swiss and Roval. Not cheap, but there are lots more wheels out there that cost more than this.

title: Giro d'Italia Women 2027 route – The complete stage-by-stage guide
author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
text:
Race organisers, RCS Sport, revealed route details for the 38th edition of the Giro d'Italia Women at a presentation in Rome on Tuesday. The race is set to take place across the country's northern regions from May 29 to June 6 in 2027.

For the second year in a row, the race will be held directly after the men's Giro d'Italia, with the first weekend of the women's race overlapping the final weekend of the men's.

This year's Giro d'Italia Women will begin in Viareggio and include one mountain time trial, two mid-mountain stages, three sprint stages, and three mountain stages (including two mountaintop finishes), with the peloton racing a total of 1,132km before finishing at Monte Bianco.

The opening day of racing is a three-star difficulty held on a circuit in Viareggio with a 124km race that includes 1,200m of elevation. The main circuit will include a climb up the Pitoro, which will be tackled four times, and the stage winner and the first pink jersey will be awarded in Viareggio.

The peloton will take on another three-star hilly race from Massa to Genova on the second day of racing. They will compete over 139km that includes two categorised ascents over the Passo del Bracco and the San Martino di Noceto before the descent into the coastal city of Genova. The stage includes 2,100m of elevation gain.

San Martino di Noceto, 112km

On the third day of racing, the peloton will tackle the longest of all the stages at 171km from Cogorno to Viadana. Although they will crest the day's only categorised ascent, Passo del Bocco at the 20km mark, it is a two-star stage, and the race is mainly downhill and undulating all the way to the finish line in Viadana. There is 1350m of elevation gain.

The first mountain test will be held on the fourth stage as the peloton takes on 131km from Credaro to the top of Passo della Presolana (Castione della Presolana), which the organisers class as four stars.

The stage will include four categorised climbs over the Forcellino di Bianzano, Ganda, Colle di Zambla and then the mountaintop summit of Passo della Presolana, an 11km climb that averages 5.4% but reaches pitches of 10% near the top. There is 3,500m of elevation gain.

Forcellino di Bianzano, 45.1km

Passo della Presolana, 131km

The only one-star stage of this nine-day race, stage 5 will surely be one for the sprinters, with only 300m of elevation gain. The peloton will take on 140km in and around Cassano d'Adda.

It is the first of two five-star stages and the second mountain finish of this race as the peloton tackles 137km from Bergamo to Madesimo-Valle Spluga. The route will include two major ascents, mid-stage over the Passo San Marco, a 19.6km climb with an average gradient of 7.4% but with pitches as steep as 15%, followed by the summit finish at Madesimo-Valle Spluga, a 19.3km ascent with an average gradient of 6.3% and maximum gradients reaching 13%. This will be a day where the race is won or lost with another 3,550m of elevation gain.

Madesimo-Valle Spluga, 137km

Stage 7 is another two-star day to give the peloton some reprieve from the climbing as they race 147km from Carugate to Rho, that includes 1,000m of elevation gain. There is only one categorised climb on the course at Sirtoti, located in the first quarter of the race.

The peloton will be treated to a mountain time trial on the penultimate day of racing. The route is held along an 11km course at Valdigne Tudor. The mid-race checkpoint is located 5.7km into the race against the clock. The 11km climb will vary between 4.2% and 9% gradient with a total of 500m of elevation gain.

The final day of racing at the Giro d'Italia Women will include 3,950m of elevation gain across 132km at Monte Bianco. There will be four categorised climbs at Doues, Verrogne, Saint-Nicolas and Colle de San Carlo, before the final climb to the finish line where the overall winner will be crowned.

The two toughest climbs of the day will be over Verrogne and Colle de San Carlo.

The ascent over Verrogne will test the riders with a stair-step ascent. The first section is 7.4Km at 7.9%, and the second section is 5.6km at 6.9%, with a 2km undulating downhill in between.

The Colle de San Carlo is a 10km climb with steep sections at the beginning that reach 15%, and the overall gradient is 9.8%.

Colle de San Carlo, 107.1km

title: Giro d'Italia Women 2027 route revealed – Uphill time trial and brutal final mountain stage feature on climber-friendly course
author: Owen Rogers
text:
The organisers of the Giro d’Italia Women unveiled the route of the 2027 race in Rome on Tuesday, and while the race is shorter than last year’s, it has far more climbing, favouring the mountain goats once again.

While this will be the 38th edition of the women’s Giro, the 2027 edition will be only the fourth organised by RCS, the company which runs the men’s event, and they continue to make the race more challenging.

In total the race is slated to cover 1,132km, some 20km shorter than last year, but with 500m more vertical ascent on the cards, and with three stages climbing 3,500m or more, the 2027 Giro will suit the purest climbers more than ever before.

Next year’s race takes place over nine stages, beginning with a lumpy opening day in the seaside resort of Viareggio on May 29, and concluding on June 6 with a brutal third Alpine road stage organisers have named the 'Monte Bianco stage', on the Italian side of Western Europe’s highest mountain, Mont Blanc. And it's a tough way to end the week the riders tackling almost 4,000m of vertical ascent.

The entire race is set in the north-west, starting in northern reaches of Tuscany before heading along the coast into Liguria. There's a brief visit to Emilia-Romagna as the race moves into Lombardy for a first visit to the mountains. The final two stages, including a mountain time trial, take place in Italy’s smallest region, the Valle d'Aosta

With such a challenging route, including two mountain top finishes, a mountain time trial and that brutal final day in the Alps, organisers will be hoping the route tempts the sport’s biggest star, Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ), to defend the maglia rosa she won last year, though whether she takes the bait is to be seen.

After her second place at the 2026 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift , it’s a race suited to Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and her new Lidl-Trek team, while after her win at the Vuelta España Femenina, the new GC star on the block, Paula Blasi, may opt for the Giro, especially as the course is suited less to her new Movistar teammate Marlen Reusser.

After finishing second overall in 2026 and with the Canyon-SRAM Scalable Capital team leadership in her hands, Antonia Niedermaier is another candidate for success, especially with the mountain time trial featuring again. However, such is the the amount of climbing , we could see pure climbers like Vuelta stage winner Petra Stiasny (Human Powered Health) and Sarah Gigante (AG Insurance-Soudal), who won two mountain stage on her way to third overall in 2025, among the suitors to the maglia rosa.

But before we get too deep into who may win, here's what the route will look like next May.

While the GC riders will need to be attentive over the three flatter opening days, the 2027 Giro will be decided over four mountain stages, which include two mountain top finishes, a time trial and the final Alpine day.

Stage 4 features four classified climbs and 3,500m of vertical ascent and the week’s first mountain top finish, stage 4 is the first GC battle of the week. Covering 131km between Credaro and Passo della Presolana, the stage heads into the Bergamasque Prealps, the day’s final climb the perfect platform for attacks with its relatively even gradient edging between 5% and 10% over almost 12km.

If one strong climber emerges on stage 4, we may see a procession two days later when stage 6 takes us into the Central Alps for another mountain top finish, this time at Madesimo above the Valle Spluga. With more climbing than the previous mountain day, the stage also includes the Cima Alfonsina Strada, the race’s highest point, the Passo San Marco, some 1,987m above sea level.

A brute of a climb, the gradient averages 7.4% over its whopping 19.6km length, though the top comes still with 80km to the finish, and ahead of the ascent to the line, which also approaches 20km in length.

The stage 8 mountain time trial will be crucial for those looking to challenge the general classification. It’s the second consecutive edition of the Giro with an uphill TT, and this is harder than the one Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) won last year, even if it’s 1.7km shorter, there's no respite over the 11km, the gradient ramping up to 10%.

The TT crosses the path of the final stage, and both will force some reshaping of the GC, though with almost 4,000m of vertical ascent in the shadow of Mont Blanc, the final day should be hugely dramatic, and could even see the GC turned on its head.

Only 132km, the day takes in four classified climbs in total, though it is the final one, the Colle San Carlo, which is likely to have the most effect, not only coming on the final day, but averaging almost 10% gradient over its 10.5km. Interestingly, it tops out 25km from the line, with a descent and a short kicker to the line, creating opportunities for some fascinating racing.

Despite the huge amount of climbing on the route, there are a good five opportunities for sprinters and opportunists.

While we could even see five bunch sprints, at least three of the days are lumpy enough to upset the fast women, and after missing out on the pink jersey after being disqualified from the 2026 Giro when her bike was judged to be underweight , Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) is likely to be disappointed with the opening stage. Starting and finishing in Viareggio, on the Tuscan coast, the 124km stage takes place over four laps, each with an early climb, and though Wiebes may be able to survive, it will be far more complicated, especially with plenty of other riders aiming for pink.

Stage 2 heads up the Ligurian coast between Massa and Genoa and is a similar lumpy day, though with much of the climbing coming early on, it’s more likely to end in a sprint than the day before. However, if a breakaway is still out front when the race reaches Genoa, the sprinters’ team will need to take care to bring it back.

At 171km, stage 3 is the longest of the nine, though, along with stage 5, it's the first of only two where a bunch sprint is almost guaranteed. A long early climb will bring a fight for the breakaway, though it will be comprised of eternal optimists, as the final 150km are downhill and the day should be easy to control on the road to Viadana.

With only 300m of climbing, stage 5 is the flattest of the week, flatter even than the time trial, and is the second nailed on opportunity for the fast women, especially if they’ve struggled for success up to that point. Another circuit race, the stage takes place around the town of Cassano d’Adda, closing with four almost pan-flat laps.

Though on the face of it stage 7 looks like another sprint day, it's sandwiched between a brutal Alpine stage and the mountain time trial, so is ripe for breakaway success. At 147km between Carugate and Rho, there is only one classified climb and some gentle undulations, so any escapees will need to work hard to the line or they’ll tempt the sprinters to take control.

title: EF Education-EasyPost Reinvents Itself as Cycling’s Super Teams Get Richer
author: ahood
text:
EF Education-EasyPost has always managed to hit big results. (Photo: Gruber Images)

EF Education-EasyPost is heading into 2027 with a smaller budget, a radical roster makeover, and some big questions about how to stay competitive in the super team era.

Richard Carapaz is gone. Longtime sports director Charly Wegelius is out. Matt White is back. And team pink is loading up on unknown talent and betting on aging stars.

The team’s DNA remains the money ball underdog in cycling’s super team era.

“I see us as a team of opportunity,” said Jonathan Vaughters , founder and CEO of EF Pro Cycling. “For young riders, we want to be the team that gives them their first real chance to excel at the WorldTour level. For others, we want to offer a second chance. Tao Geoghegan Hart is a great example of that.”

The financial arms race in the WorldTour isn’t slowing down, so EF is adapting.

UAE Emirates-XRG, Visma-Lease a Bike, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and Lidl-Trek continue to stack their rosters with expensive stars and emerging talent.

Vaughters knows EF — which packs a middle-of-the-peloton budget — cannot win a bidding war against cycling’s deepest pockets.

The challenge is finding riders the super teams overlook and try to develop young talent before their price tags explode, and then deliver results when and where the argyle army can.

“But more than anything, I want every rider on this team to have an opportunity to shine. We’re not going to build our entire racing strategy around protecting individual leaders,” he said. “We want to race openly and give everyone the freedom to take their chances.”

It’s the latest shape-shifting for a team that has long punched above its financial weight against the sport’s richest teams.

The long-running U.S. team — dating back to 2007 — has never had the biggest budget in the peloton, and now it’s facing its latest challenge to remain competitive just as deep-pocketed teams keep piling on .

Carapaz still had another year on his contract, but EF agreed to release him early .

“We willingly let Richie go. It was not forced,” Vaughters told the Escape Collective . “We needed to make some hard decisions … A very simple option would be to just let your most highly compensated rider leave.”

Carapaz is not the only big-name departure as the team tries to find a space to remain competitive without blowing out the bank.

Georg Steinhauser, one of the team’s most promising young climbers, is heading to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

Classics specialists Kasper Asgreen and Michael Valgren are also leaving, along with Madis Mihkels, Mikkel Honoré, James Shaw, and rising Spanish talent Markel Beloki.

The departures of some of the team’s most prolific performers means the team will have to reshuffle its racing style for next season.

“We’re going to be opportunistic, to see possibilities that other teams might miss. We’ve always raced that way, but in 2027, we’re going to take it even further,” Vaughters said. “I think that’s something really unique in the WorldTour.”

Vaughters is hoping to find space between the bidding wars at the top to carve out some wins by racing against the odds.

The upheaval isn’t limited to the roster.

Wegelius, one of EF’s most influential sports directors, is leaving after 15 seasons with the organization.

The Briton joined the former Garmin setup in 2012 and his departure follows other changes in the management structure, including the exits of Tejay Van Garderen and Matti Breschel.

Coming in is Australian veteran Matt White , who returns to the team where he launched his sports director career in 2008 after stints at Jayco-AlUla and Movistar.

White joins an established group of sports directors, including Juanma Gárate, Carmen Small, Tom Southam, Daniel Foder, Andreas Klier, Michael Creed, Huub Duijn, Ken Vanmarcke, and Sebastian Langeveld. Recently retired Dan McLay also joins as a sport director.

“I genuinely believe we have the best group of people working behind the scenes of any team in the WorldTour,” Vaughters said. “Our goal is to connect all of those dots, from the moment we first identify a promising young rider to the moment they’re competing for victories at the biggest races in the world. That’s how we build a team that can win today and continue getting better in the years ahead.”

White and the other sport directors will have pressure to deliver results right out of the gate.

The team will have one eye on the UCI team rankings. Coming out of 2026 in the first season of a three-year WorldTour cycle, EF was ranked 15th among teams chasing points to secure its next WorldTour license at the end of 2028.

With a spending war playing out across the peloton, Vaughters and EF’s brain trust have targeted riders with something to prove.

Former Giro d’Italia champion Geoghegan Hart arrives from Lidl-Trek while Colombian climber Iván Sosa returns to the WorldTour.

German prospect Emil Herzog joins from Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe on a deal through 2029 and Tobias Bayer brings classics experience from Alpecin, while young American Gavin Sherry is among several riders stepping up from the team’s development program.

“We have a really exciting opportunity to build something special with the young talent coming through our program,” Vaughters said. “EF Education-Aevolo is a big part of that, but it’s also about the riders and staff we already have at the WorldTour level. We’ve had the youngest team in the WorldTour for a few years now, and we intend to continue that.”

It’s a calculated gamble on two fronts. Riders like Herzog and Sherry represent EF’s future, while Geoghegan Hart and Sosa see a chance to revive stalled careers.

If even one or two deliver, EF could find some serious payback in a transfer market dominated by bigger spenders.

Ben Healy and Neilson Powless remain as the men’s team’s most important anchors heading into 2027.…

title: Do Ferrari need rules of engagement? F1 Q&A
text:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest world champion by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the race, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton finishing second.

Hamilton was unhappy with his team-mate Charles Leclerc and said Ferrari "have to have some serious talks behind closed doors" after fighting between their two drivers cost them victory in Mexico.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

McLaren has its 'papaya' rules, is it now time for Ferrari to introduce its 'Maranello' rules? - John

The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc on the opening lap in Mexico, and the fall-out from it, provided a perfect illustration of the problems that can arise when a team has two top drivers of equal status.

Hamilton's point after the race was that Ferrari would have won the race - probably got a one-two - if the pair had worked together on that first lap.

"When your team-mate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough," he said.

Team boss Frederic Vasseur aldo bemoaned the loss of a potential one-two, admitting he was "frustrated".

Leclerc argued that it takes two to tango. "I could be also unhappy with how much he pushed me off track out of Turn One," he said, "but it is racing. When you are fighting for a win it is the way it should be."

Leclerc added: "At the end we both did a mistake going into Turn Four. It's not like we had contact whatsoever. We both went straight and that gave the opportunity for Max to overtake. So I don't think it should be that much of a talking point."

Clearly there is a problem here. It's not the first time the Ferrari drivers' competing priorities have caused issues this year, and Vasseur has yet to find a way to manage it effectively, and get the drivers to buy into what he decides.

In this case, the two drivers are expressing two completely different, but valid, points of view.

Hamilton is thinking of the team result - which conveniently also meant a win for him - Leclerc primarily about the fact that they are allowed to race for the win.

The problem is that the team's result was compromised and a win thrown away.

Had Verstappen not passed Hamilton as a consequence of the incident, Leclerc could have given the place back by Turn 11 as was required by the rules.

But once Verstappen was between them, continuing in the lead was Leclerc's only realistic option.

This is a really difficult situation for Vasseur to handle.

The team wants to win the race as first priority, but the same applies to each individual driver. Sometimes those two competing priorities clash.

And if Ferrari ever get themselves a car that can compete for the title, it will only get harder, because the stakes for both drivers are then much higher.

McLaren have done better at handling this, and Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have been more acquiescent, but even their approach has led them into problems, as happened a number of times last year. And sometimes the drivers ignore it, as with the crash between the two drivers in the sprint in Singapore.

Vasseur's problem is that if he had asked the drivers not to race on the first lap on Sunday, he would have been essentially asking Leclerc to hand Hamilton a win. And how do you keep an ambitious driver happy in that situation?

One also has to ask whether, if the situations were reversed, Hamilton would accept the same request.

Hamilton revealed after the race that Ferrari "don't have rules of engagement, and whether or not that would change anything from Charles' side, I don't know".

McLaren have rules of engagement. One is not to crash into each other. That's not what happened here. Another is that the team result comes first. But it's very hard to come up with specific rules that would deal with a live racing situation such as this.

One could argue all day about the rights and wrongs and who could have done what to engineer a better outcome.

As Hamilton said: "We've just got to figure out. But something needs to change for sure."

Given that Yamaha have withdrawn from MotoGP in Qatar (and, I understand, much of the media aren't going), why is F1 still so intent on going? The US mid-terms are potentially a trigger point. The risk seems too high. - Richard

This weekend's Qatar MotoGP has been a subject of controversy in motorcycle racing in the context of the war in the Middle East.

First, the vast majority of riders wrote a letter to the sport's bosses saying they would prefer not to race there, and at the weekend Yamaha pulled out of the race, citing a company-wide travel policy.

The race is still going ahead. MotoGP, like F1, is owned by US group Liberty Media.

Similar concerns also exist within F1 on a widespread basis about the end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi going ahead.

Privately, many people within the sport have significant misgivings about going to the Middle East, but those opinions are by and large not being voiced publicly.

One person who has done so is Williams driver Carlos Sainz, who said at the US Grand Prix: "(The sport's bosses) seem very convinced that it's going to go ahead.

"On my personal side, and not speaking as the GPDA, it's very difficult to be convinced right now because there are still things happening in the Middle East, and also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US and things that are going to happen on the political side of the world that could affect the next month, month and a half, very suddenly.

"So, I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced."

It's hard to argue with the factual basis for those remarks. Nevertheless, Sainz and Williams were subsequently spoken to by F1, after which Williams put out a statement "clarifying" his remarks.

F1's argument is that it has no reason to cancel the races.…

title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
text:
Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.

On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.

Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.

Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.

During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.

Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."

In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket.

Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three.

Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years.

"I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."

Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds.

"Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.

Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay.

Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year".

While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online.

Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on TikTok of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells.

She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600.

"I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."

Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."

For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them.

This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money."

Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items.

Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says.

But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?

Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita.

"Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.

In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external .

In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances.

"In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.

"But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying
author: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston and Spoorthy Raman
text:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.

This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.

Documents obtained by the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay under the UK’s Freedom of Information Act reveal Vantara’s efforts to lobby British officials and ministers before the meeting.

Ambani, 31, is the heir to the oil and gas fortune of one of India’s richest men, Mukesh Ambani. He set up a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near his family’s oil-refining facilities in Gujarat, where more than 150,000 animals have reportedly been amassed since 2022. Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care, including facilities such as an elephant hydrotherapy pool , where more than 260 elephants can also receive oil therapies and Ayurvedic massage.

But conservation groups have repeatedly questioned how such a vast number of species, many of which are endangered, were gathered so quickly. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing.

A subsequent Cites fact-finding mission looking into the zoo raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.

Its November 2025 report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”

In May, officials from the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) met a representative from Vantara and the US lobbyist firm Checkmate Government Relations, founded by Ches McDowell, a hunting friend of Donald Trump Jr.

Before the meeting, internal briefing documents said Checkmate was “seeking to persuade the UK to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara and of Checkmate’s argument that responsibility for verifying legality sits primarily with exporting or re-exporting parties rather than with India as importer”.

During the meeting, the Vantara representative invited UK officials to visit the zoo – an invitation that was subsequently declined to ensure the impartiality of the UK’s Cites chair role.

After the meeting, a representative from another lobbying firm, Atlas Strategy, working on behalf of Vantara, approached the then secretary of state, Emma Reynolds, and then nature minister, Mary Creagh, also raising the prospect of a visit to the zoo.

When Reynolds asked for advice, a note was issued recommending that ministers did not engage formally with Vantara.

The government documents also reveal concerns about an application by Vantara to import falcons and falcon hybrids, after an unnamed organisation made a £50,000 “donation” to a breeder in the UK, whose identity was also not disclosed. British Cites officials classified the transaction as commercial, according to the documents. The falcons were not exported to India.

A spokesperson for Vantara said it had not imported falcons from the UK, nor had the zoo hired or paid a lobbying firm. It is understood that Checkmate and Altas Strategy were working pro bono for Vantara and not required to register with the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists.

After recent scrutiny, Vantara has sought to “reset” its activities by voluntarily suspending animal imports for a year and hiring John Scanlon, a former Cites chief, to oversee its operations. In an interview with the Sunday Times this year, Ambani said he only brought animals to Vantara legally to ensure their welfare, mentioning a group of hippos he had saved from a hunting lodge in South Africa and jackass penguins saved from a shopping centre in Qatar.

“I think since I was a baby I have been taking care of animals. It’s always been a passion,” he said.

Vantara was used to host Ambani’s lavish pre-wedding celebrations in 2024 , which were attended by celebrity guests and politicians. In September, Newcastle University awarded the oil heir a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship”, sparking a backlash from conservationists.

A Defra spokesperson said: “The UK has strict rules in place to protect endangered species and ensuring international wildlife trade is legal and sustainable, with every application assessed individually against internationally agreed and domestic requirements.”

title: British Airways lost my father’s vital life-saving machine
author: Anna Tims
text:
He needs a dialysis machine to survive, but on a flight it was first damaged, then it was lost

My father suffers from terminal renal failure and relies on a highly specific dialysis machine every night to survive. British Airways’ check-in staff twice insisted on checking this fragile 20kg lifeline into the aircraft hold where it was first damaged, then lost.

When his outbound flight arrived at Heathrow, it was returned broken resulting in a frantic search for a loan unit and hours spent in A&E so my father’s blood could be monitored. On the return flight to Rome, the machine could not be found. My parents waited until 2am before being told to go home without the equipment that keeps my father alive.

He had to borrow another unit from a hospital. His was finally delivered three days later with the protective case unsealed and critical internal components disconnected.

The sheer terror and stress of missing a treatment, not knowing if the A&E could accommodate him in time, and fearing that his health had already been severely compromised, was indescribable.

British Airways has missed all deadlines to address our complaint and is now ignoring our correspondence. DL , London

Your father did not need to use the fragile unit during the flight but was concerned, rightly as it turned out, it might suffer damage in the hold.

BA, in common with most airlines, allows vital medical equipment to travel for free along with its owner, provided it does not exceed the dimensions of cabin baggage. It’s essential for safety reasons that belongings can be stowed under a seat or an overhead locker.

Your father’s device was too large, and I believe it was reasonable for BA to check it into the hold if the flight was full. If, however, there were spare seats, it could have allowed it to travel on one. It has since told you a seat could have been bought.

The real shocker is that such vital kit was mishandled not once, but twice. The impact on your father could have been grave had loan units not been found. BA’s response was, at best, cavalier.

When you wrote to me, a month had passed since your initial complaint and you’d heard nothing besides auto-generated acknowledgments.

The company got its act together when I questioned its attitude. An operative called you to apologise and it managed, at last, to reply to your emails. However, you are unimpressed by its offer of £300 in e-vouchers to, in its words, “put things right”. I’ve suggested it convert this into cash and consider a sum that better reflects the impact on your father. It told me it will be in touch to discuss a “gesture”.
